Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no “Is the lung healthy?” answer whose rationale cites a claimed prior/grounded report finding—such as “Lungs are clear”—but the transcript contains no raw tool observation documenting that lung finding (as here, observations are empty).

Observable verification action: Before finalizing, search the raw tool outputs for an explicit same-object/same-attribute statement about the lungs or parenchyma. If absent, do not present the claimed report language as observed evidence; rerun or consult the grounded-report/chest-X-ray tool and inspect its actual output. Base the final Yes/No only on that documented lung finding: if it explicitly documents a lung abnormality such as infiltrate, consolidation, effusion, or nodule, answer No; if it explicitly states the lungs are clear with no parenchymal abnormality, answer Yes. If options are present, map the supported answer text back to the displayed choice and check that the letter and text agree. In this case options were empty, so the key check is evidence attribution: the cited “Lungs are clear” statement was not present in any recorded observation, so the correct released answer alone does not verify the evidence path.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no answer to “Is the lung healthy?” from a grounded chest X-ray report, especially when the report also contains incidental non-lung findings such as a PICC line or catheter.

Observable verification action: Re-read the raw grounded-report observation and confirm that the terminal rationale cites an explicit lung/parenchymal abnormality—for example, “bilateral lower lobe infiltrates”—rather than an incidental device or unrelated finding. For a “No” answer, require at least one lung-relevant abnormality in the report and confirm the final polarity matches it. If no such finding is present, revise the rationale or answer, or obtain the missing observation. If answer choices are displayed, map the supported answer text back to the displayed option and verify that its letter and text agree; if options are empty, only the evidence check applies. In this case, the report explicitly contains “Bilateral lower lobe infiltrates,” so the answer “No” is supported; the PICC-line finding is not needed for the lung-health judgment.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no “Is the lung healthy?” answer and the draft rationale cites specific imaging findings—such as pleural effusions or atelectasis—but the current trajectory has no raw image/report/tool observation explicitly documenting those findings for the lung.

Observable verification action: Re-read the available raw tool observations and confirm that at least one explicitly names the same organ/attribute and supports each cited abnormality. If such an observation is present, use it and confirm the final yes/no polarity matches it. If it is absent, do not present the finding as observed evidence; revise the rationale to a documented finding or retrieve/rerun the necessary observation before finalizing. If contradictory observations exist, resolve them before choosing. In this case, “No” matched the released reference, but the rationale cited bilateral pleural effusions and right lung base atelectasis while the observations were empty, so the correct grade alone does not verify the evidence path. If options were displayed, map the supported answer text back to the listed choice and check that its letter and text agree.
